A 3-week-old male infant is brought to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of lethargy. He
was born at home via an unattended spontaneous vaginal delivery at approximately 39 weeks of
gestation and has not previously seen a healthcare provider. There was no prenatal care during the
pregnancy. The parents report no fever, rash, vomiting, or diarrhea. Before this episode, the infant had
been breastfeeding well with normal urine and stool output. His temperature is 98.7 ºF, blood pressure
is 87/59 mmHg, pulse is 129/min, and respiratory rate is 22/min. On examination, the infant is lethargic
and unresponsive to painful stimuli. He is intubated for airway protection, and a full laboratory and
imaging workup is performed. Laboratory results show a normal platelet count, severely prolonged
prothrombin time, prolonged partial thromboplastin time, and prolonged clotting time. Which of the
following best explains the most likely cause of this infant’s condition? Answer Choices: (A) Neonatal
sepsis with coagulopathy (B) Hepatic immaturity (C) Maternal vitamin K deficiency (D) Infantile
botulism (E) Early-onset Group B streptococcal infection (F) Disseminated intravascular coagulation
(G) Inherited factor VII deficiency (H) Congenital protein C deficiency (I) Immature microbiome (J)
Congenital toxoplasmosis
 A. Congenital toxoplasmosis
B. Inherited factor VII deficiency
C. Maternal vitamin K deficiency
D. Hepatic immaturity
E. Congenital protein C deficiency
F. Immature microbiome
G. Early-onset Group B streptococcal infection
H. Infantile botulism

I. Disseminated intravascular coagulation
J. Neonatal sepsis with coagulopathy
